# Persuasion and Communication {#persuasion-communication}

Why does a car manufacturer fill its print advertisements with fuel-economy
figures, crash-test ratings, and warranty terms, while a chewing-gum brand runs a
thirty-second spot with a catchy jingle and a famous face? Why does a sponsored
post from an influencer persuade some followers and irritate others, and why does
the word "#ad" sometimes change how the very same message is received? Why do some
stories spread through social networks within hours while carefully produced
corporate content goes unseen? And why can a single choice of words, "95% fat
free" rather than "5% fat", "lives saved" rather than "lives lost", reverse what
people prefer?

Each puzzle concerns how messages change minds, and each has been addressed by a
distinct theoretical tradition. Social psychology contributed **[dual-process](#dual-process-theory) (Section \@ref(dual-process-theory))
models of persuasion**, which explain when people scrutinise arguments and when
they rely on cues. Consumer research added the **[persuasion knowledge model](#persuasion-knowledge-model)**,
which treats audiences as active agents who recognise and cope with influence
attempts. Marketing and sociology developed theories of **[word of mouth](#social-transmission) and social
transmission**, which ask why people pass information on. Mass-communication
research produced **[agenda setting](#agenda-setting)**, **framing**, and **uses and
gratifications**, which explain what media make salient, how they package issues,
and why audiences choose the media they do. This chapter develops each tradition,
shows how they connect, and translates them into hypotheses and managerial
practice (Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-glance)).

```{r tab-pc-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "Elaboration likelihood model", "When do arguments, rather than cues, change attitudes?", "Individual", "Petty & Cacioppo (1986)",
  "Heuristic-systematic model", "How do heuristic and systematic processing combine?", "Individual", "Chaiken (1980)",
  "Persuasion knowledge model", "How do targets recognise and cope with influence attempts?", "Individual / dyad", "Friestad & Wright (1994)",
  "Social transmission (word of mouth)", "Why do people share, and what gets shared?", "Individual / network", "Berger (2014)",
  "Two-step flow", "How does media influence travel through interpersonal ties?", "Network / community", "Katz & Lazarsfeld (1955)",
  "Undirected communication (microblogging)", "Why broadcast to no one in particular?", "Individual", "Buechel & Berger (2017)",
  "Agenda setting", "How do media shape what the public thinks is important?", "Society / public", "McCombs & Shaw (1972)",
  "Framing", "How does the packaging of information change judgment?", "Individual / society", "Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Entman (1993)",
  "Uses and gratifications", "Why do audiences choose the media they do?", "Individual", "Katz, Blumler & Gurevitch (1973)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of persuasion and communication.")
```

Two organising ideas recur throughout. First, **receivers are not passive**. The
earliest research on mass communication imagined messages as injections whose
effects could be read off their content. Each theory in this chapter replaces that
image with an active audience: one that decides how much effort to invest
(dual-process models), interprets the sender's motives (persuasion knowledge),
selects and passes on content for its own reasons (social transmission, uses and
gratifications), and constructs meaning from the frames it encounters. Second,
**effects are conditional**. None of these theories predicts that a message will
work everywhere. Each specifies the moderators, involvement, accessibility of
motives, emotional arousal, issue obtrusiveness, audience goals, that determine
when it will.

## The Elaboration Likelihood Model {#elaboration-likelihood-model}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Attitudes can change through two qualitatively different routes.
When people are motivated and able to think about a message, persuasion depends on
the quality of its arguments (the **central route**). When motivation or ability is
low, persuasion depends on simple cues such as source attractiveness or the number
of arguments (the **peripheral route**).

**Origins.** Social psychology. @petty1986, building on the Yale communication
programme [@hovland1953] and cognitive-response research. First tested in an
advertising context by @petty1983.

**Level of analysis.** Individual message recipient.

**Key constructs.** Elaboration likelihood, motivation (personal relevance,
involvement, need for cognition), ability (distraction, repetition, prior
knowledge), argument quality, peripheral cues, attitude strength.

**Boundary conditions.** Assumes recipients hold or form an attitude toward a
definable object. Applies most directly to message-based influence. Predictions
about route depend on accurately measuring or manipulating elaboration rather than
inferring it from outcomes.

**Related theories.** [Heuristic-systematic model](#heuristic-systematic-model),
[Persuasion knowledge model](#persuasion-knowledge-model),
[Dual-process theory](#dual-process-theory) (Section \@ref(dual-process-theory)),
[Processing fluency](#processing-fluency) (Section \@ref(processing-fluency)), [Mere exposure](#mere-exposure-effect) (Section \@ref(mere-exposure-effect)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The Yale Communication Research Program after the Second World War organised
persuasion research around the question "who says what to whom with what effect",
and studied source credibility, message order, fear appeals, and audience
characteristics as separate variables [@hovland1953]. The programme produced a
large body of findings but also a frustrating pattern: the same variable, an
expert source, a long message, a fear appeal, sometimes increased persuasion,
sometimes had no effect, and sometimes backfired. By the 1970s, the field lacked a
framework for predicting *which* outcome would occur.

@petty1986 proposed that the inconsistencies arose because researchers had not
taken into account how much recipients were thinking. They defined
**elaboration** as the extent to which a person thinks about the issue-relevant
arguments contained in a message, and argued that elaboration likelihood varies
along a continuum. At the high end, people scrutinise arguments, generate their own
favourable or unfavourable thoughts, and integrate those thoughts into an attitude.
At the low end, people form attitudes by applying simple inferences, "experts are
usually right", "if so many arguments are offered, the position must be sound", or
through affective associations. Variables such as source expertise therefore have
different effects at different levels of elaboration.

### Core logic and propositions

The model can be summarised in a set of propositions that correspond closely to
the postulates set out by @petty1986:

- **P1 (Correctness motive).** People are motivated to hold correct attitudes,
  but the amount of effort they are willing or able to devote to evaluating a
  message varies with individual and situational factors.
- **P2 (Elaboration continuum).** Elaboration varies continuously from low to high.
  The two "routes" describe the endpoints of this continuum rather than two
  discrete boxes.
- **P3 (Trade-off).** As elaboration increases, the impact of argument quality on
  attitudes increases and the impact of peripheral cues decreases.
- **P4 (Multiple roles).** A single variable can affect persuasion in different
  ways: it can serve as an argument, act as a peripheral cue, influence the amount
  of elaboration, or bias the direction of elaboration.
- **P5 (Attitude strength).** Attitudes formed or changed through the central route
  are more persistent over time, more resistant to counter-persuasion, and more
  predictive of behaviour than attitudes changed through the peripheral route.

::: {.definition}
**Argument quality** is defined empirically in ELM research: strong arguments are
those that, when people are instructed to think about them, elicit predominantly
favourable thoughts. Weak arguments elicit predominantly unfavourable thoughts.
**Peripheral cues** are features of the persuasion context that allow an attitude
judgment without scrutiny of the issue-relevant merits: source attractiveness,
celebrity, the sheer number of arguments, audience applause.
:::

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pc-elm-routes) traces the two routes. Motivation and ability
act as gatekeepers. If both are present, the recipient processes the arguments and
the valence of the resulting thoughts drives attitude change. If either is
missing, the recipient looks for a peripheral cue. Note the dashed path in the
figure: when no cue is present, or when cognitive processing produces no net
change, the person retains the initial attitude.

```{r fig-pc-elm-routes, fig.cap = "The elaboration likelihood model. Motivation and ability determine whether a message is processed centrally (argument scrutiny, enduring attitude change) or peripherally (cue-based, temporary change). Adapted from the logic in Petty and Cacioppo (1986)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  M  [label = "Persuasive\\nmessage", %s]
  MO [label = "Motivation to process?\\n(relevance, need for cognition)", %s]
  AB [label = "Ability to process?\\n(distraction, knowledge, time)", %s]
  CT [label = "Argument scrutiny:\\nfavourable vs. unfavourable\\nthoughts", %s]
  PC [label = "Peripheral cue present?\\n(source, number of arguments)", %s]
  CE [label = "Central-route change:\\nenduring, resistant,\\npredicts behaviour", %s]
  PE [label = "Peripheral-route change:\\ntemporary, susceptible", %s]
  RI [label = "Retain or regain\\ninitial attitude", %s]
  M -> MO
  MO -> AB [label = " yes"]
  AB -> CT [label = " yes"]
  CT -> CE
  MO -> PC [label = " no", style = dashed]
  AB -> PC [label = " no", style = dashed]
  PC -> PE [label = " yes"]
  PC -> RI [label = " no", style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_moderator, node_moderator, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_outcome, node_construct), rankdir = "TB")
```

The signature prediction of the model is an **interaction** between elaboration
and message features. The best-known demonstration is @petty1983, who showed
participants a magazine advertisement for a disposable razor. Involvement was
manipulated by telling some participants that the product would soon be available
in their area and that they would later choose among razor brands (high
involvement), and telling others the product would not be available locally (low
involvement). The advertisement contained either strong or weak arguments and was
endorsed either by famous athletes or by ordinary citizens. Argument quality had a
much larger effect on attitudes under high involvement, whereas the celebrity
endorsement mattered more under low involvement. An earlier study had found the
same pattern for argument quality versus source expertise in a policy context:
students evaluating a proposal to introduce comprehensive examinations either at
their own university next year (high relevance) or at some later date [@petty1981].

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pc-elm-interaction) illustrates the crossover logic with
simulated data. The two panels are mirror images: the factor that matters most
under high involvement (argument quality) matters least under low involvement,
and vice versa for the peripheral cue.

```{r fig-pc-elm-interaction, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of the ELM interaction. Under high involvement, argument quality drives attitudes and the endorser matters little. Under low involvement, the pattern reverses. Points are cell means with 95% confidence intervals. Data are simulated, not empirical.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1983)
cells <- expand.grid(involvement = c("Low involvement", "High involvement"),
                     level = c("high", "low"),
                     factor = c("Argument quality varied", "Endorser (peripheral cue) varied"),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cells$mu <- with(cells, ifelse(factor == "Argument quality varied",
  ifelse(involvement == "High involvement", ifelse(level == "high", 1.6, -0.9), ifelse(level == "high", 0.5, 0.1)),
  ifelse(involvement == "High involvement", ifelse(level == "high", 0.45, 0.25), ifelse(level == "high", 1.1, -0.4))))
sim <- cells[rep(seq_len(nrow(cells)), each = 40), ]
sim$attitude <- rnorm(nrow(sim), sim$mu, 1.2)
elm <- sim |>
  group_by(factor, involvement, level) |>
  summarise(m = mean(attitude), se = sd(attitude) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(involvement = factor(involvement, levels = c("Low involvement", "High involvement")),
         label = case_when(
           factor == "Argument quality varied" & level == "high" ~ "Strong arguments",
           factor == "Argument quality varied" ~ "Weak arguments",
           level == "high" ~ "Celebrity endorser",
           TRUE ~ "Ordinary endorser"))
ggplot(elm, aes(involvement, m, group = label, colour = level)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se), size = 0.35) +
  geom_text(data = filter(elm, involvement == "High involvement"),
            aes(label = label), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.08, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~factor) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(high = pal[["blue"]], low = pal[["orange"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 1.3))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attitude toward the product (standardised)",
       title = "What persuades depends on how much people think",
       caption = "Illustrative: simulated data (n = 40 per cell), patterned on the design of Petty, Cacioppo, & Schumann (1983).")
```

### The heuristic-systematic model {#heuristic-systematic-model}

The ELM's closest relative is the **heuristic-systematic model** (HSM), developed
by @chaiken1980 and elaborated in @eagly1993. **Systematic processing** is a
comprehensive, analytic treatment of judgment-relevant information.
**Heuristic processing** applies simple decision rules ("experts can be trusted",
"consensus implies correctness") that are stored in memory and cued by the
situation. In her original experiments, Chaiken manipulated recipients' issue
involvement together with the likability of the communicator and the number of
arguments in the message. Communicator likability mattered more when involvement
was low, whereas the content of the arguments carried more weight when
involvement was high [@chaiken1980].

The two models are often treated as interchangeable, but they differ in emphasis.
The HSM's **sufficiency principle** holds that people exert as much effort as needed
to reach a desired level of judgmental confidence, and its **co-occurrence
assumption** holds that the two modes can operate simultaneously: heuristic cues
can add to systematic processing, be attenuated by it, or bias it by shaping how
ambiguous arguments are interpreted. Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-elm-hsm) compares the
models.

```{r tab-pc-elm-hsm}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Elaboration likelihood model`, ~`Heuristic-systematic model`,
  "Key source", "Petty & Cacioppo (1986)", "Chaiken (1980), Eagly & Chaiken (1993)",
  "Low-effort mode", "Peripheral route: any cue-based process (heuristics, affect, conditioning)", "Heuristic processing: application of stored decision rules",
  "High-effort mode", "Central route: scrutiny of issue-relevant arguments", "Systematic processing: comprehensive analysis of information",
  "Relation between modes", "Trade-off: cue impact falls as elaboration rises", "Co-occurrence: modes can add, attenuate, or bias one another",
  "What drives effort", "Motivation and ability", "Sufficiency principle: gap between actual and desired confidence",
  "Motives considered", "Primarily accuracy (correct attitudes)", "Accuracy, defence, and impression motives",
  "Signature concept", "Multiple roles of a single variable", "Biased systematic processing",
  "Typical managerial reading", "Match creative strategy to involvement", "Use cues that also shape how arguments are read"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Two dual-process models of persuasion compared.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The dual-process framework is among the most heavily tested in social psychology.
Several lines of evidence stand out:

- **Involvement.** A meta-analysis by @johnson1989 found that the type of
  involvement matters. *Outcome-relevant* involvement (the issue has consequences
  for one's goals) interacts with argument quality in the way the ELM predicts,
  whereas *value-relevant* involvement (the issue engages core values) tends to
  reduce persuasion regardless of argument quality, because people defend their
  existing positions.
- **Individual differences.** People high in **need for cognition**, a stable
  tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking, are more influenced by
  argument quality and less by peripheral cues [@cacioppo1982].
- **Multiple roles.** The same variable can play different roles. An attractive
  endorser is a peripheral cue for a low-involvement snack, but an *argument* for a
  beauty product whose benefit is appearance. Under moderate elaboration, a
  surprising source can increase scrutiny itself [@petty1986].
- **Attitude strength.** Central-route attitudes are more durable and better
  predictors of behaviour, which is why the quality of the attitude, not only its
  valence, matters for long-run outcomes such as repeat purchase.

::: {.debate}
**One route or two?** @kruglanski1999 argued in their **unimodel** that cues and
arguments are not processed by different routes at all: both are "evidence" from
which people draw conclusions, and the apparent dual-route pattern arises because
studies typically present cues briefly and early and arguments at length and later.
When cue information is made as lengthy and complex as argument information, the
unimodel predicts that it, too, will matter most under high elaboration. Defenders
of the dual-process view reply that the ELM was always defined in terms of the
*process* (scrutiny of merits versus simple inference) rather than the *content*
type, and that the multiple-roles postulate already anticipates a cue acting as an
argument. The debate remains instructive for researchers: claims about "route" must
be supported by process evidence, thought listings, argument-quality
manipulations, response latencies, rather than inferred from which variable
happened to predict attitudes.
:::

### Applications in business

The ELM translates directly into decisions about creative strategy, media
selection, and sales communication. The core managerial question is not "which
message is best?" but "how much will this audience be thinking when it encounters
the message?"

::: {.business-case}
**Ad creative for high- versus low-involvement categories.** Categories differ
systematically in the elaboration they invite. A buyer comparing mortgages,
enterprise software, or family cars faces significant financial and performance
risk. The buyer is motivated to scrutinise claims and often has time to do so.
Communication in these categories typically leads with verifiable arguments,
specifications, total cost of ownership, independent ratings, case studies, and
supplies them in formats that support processing (comparison tables, configurators,
white papers). By contrast, a shopper choosing chewing gum, soft drinks, or
snacks is rarely motivated to read argument-heavy copy. Advertising in these
categories leans on cues that operate with minimal thought: celebrity and
likeable characters, music, humour, brand repetition, and packaging that is easy
to recognise at shelf. The ELM also explains why the *same* category can require
both approaches. A first-time buyer of a smartphone may be highly involved,
whereas a loyal repeat buyer is not. Brands therefore pair detailed launch
communications with simpler reminder advertising.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The effect of argument strength on brand attitude will be stronger when
  purchase is imminent (high outcome-relevant involvement) than when it is distant.
- *H2.* The effect of influencer popularity on purchase intention will be stronger
  for low-priced than for high-priced products.
- *H3.* Attitudes formed after argument-rich advertising will predict repeat
  purchase better than equally favourable attitudes formed after cue-based
  advertising.

**Designs.** Factorial experiments that cross argument quality with a motivation or
ability manipulation (relevance, distraction, time pressure). Field experiments
that vary creative executions across audiences with different involvement.
Thought-listing protocols to measure elaboration directly.

**Measures.** Thought listing and cognitive-response coding, need for cognition
scale [@cacioppo1982], attitude strength (certainty, accessibility, resistance to
counter-messages), recall of arguments versus cues.

**Contexts.** Advertising pretesting, health communication, sales presentations,
online reviews (review content as arguments, star ratings as cues), and
recommendation interfaces.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Inferring the route from the result.** A common misuse is to observe that a cue
predicted attitudes and conclude that people "used the peripheral route", or that
argument quality predicted attitudes and conclude that they "used the central
route". This is circular. Route should be established independently, by
manipulating motivation or ability, or by measuring elaboration, and the theory's
evidence is the *interaction* between elaboration and message features, not a main
effect of either.
:::

## The Persuasion Knowledge Model {#persuasion-knowledge-model}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers develop knowledge about persuasion, what marketers and
other agents are trying to do, how their tactics work, and how to respond, and use
that knowledge to interpret and cope with influence attempts. Recognising a
behaviour as a persuasion tactic can change its meaning and its effect.

**Origins.** Consumer research, @friestad1994, tested and extended by
@campbell2000.

**Level of analysis.** Individual target and dyad (target and persuasion agent).

**Key constructs.** Target, agent, persuasion attempt, persuasion episode,
persuasion knowledge, agent knowledge, topic knowledge, coping behaviour,
change-of-meaning principle, accessibility of ulterior motives, cognitive capacity.

**Boundary conditions.** Persuasion knowledge must be available (learned) and
accessible (activated) at the moment of exposure, and the target must have the
capacity to apply it. Children, novices, and distracted consumers use it less.

**Related theories.** [Elaboration likelihood model](#elaboration-likelihood-model),
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)), [Heuristics and
biases](#heuristics-biases) (Section \@ref(heuristics-biases)).
:::

### Core logic

@friestad1994 reframed persuasion from the target's point of view. Earlier theories
asked how a message changes an attitude. The persuasion knowledge model (PKM) asks
how ordinary people make sense of the fact that someone is trying to influence them.
Over a lifetime, consumers acquire folk theories about advertising, selling,
negotiation, and social influence: why agents do what they do, which tactics are
fair, and which signal manipulation. These beliefs form **persuasion knowledge**,
one of three knowledge structures that targets bring to an encounter (Table
\@ref(tab:tab-pc-pkm)).

```{r tab-pc-pkm}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Knowledge structure`, ~`What it contains`, ~`Example question the target asks`, ~`Business illustration`,
  "Persuasion knowledge", "Beliefs about agents' goals and tactics, their effectiveness, and their appropriateness", "\"Why is this salesperson complimenting me?\"", "Recognising scarcity claims as a pressure tactic",
  "Agent knowledge", "Beliefs about the specific agent's traits, competence, and goals", "\"Is this brand trustworthy?\"", "Prior experience with a retailer's return policy",
  "Topic knowledge", "Beliefs about the product, issue, or service being promoted", "\"Do these specifications make sense?\"", "An engineer evaluating a component supplier's claims"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The three knowledge structures in the persuasion knowledge model (after Friestad & Wright, 1994).")
```

Two ideas carry most of the model's predictive power. The first is the
**change-of-meaning principle**: once a target recognises an agent's action as a
persuasion tactic, the action can acquire a different meaning. Flattery that seemed
sincere becomes ingratiation, a "limited-time offer" becomes a pressure tactic, a
glowing product mention becomes advertising. The second idea is that targets are
**coping**, not merely reacting. Their goal is to manage the episode in a way that
serves their own interests, sometimes resisting, sometimes accepting the message
while discounting the source, sometimes enjoying a clever tactic for what it is.

### Mechanism

Persuasion knowledge does not operate automatically. @campbell2000 showed that its
use depends on the **accessibility** of the agent's ulterior motive and on the
target's **cognitive capacity**. In their studies, consumers who encountered a
salesperson's flattery were more likely to infer an ulterior motive when the motive
was highly accessible, for example, when the flattery came *before* a purchase
decision rather than after, and cognitively busy targets were less likely to draw
on persuasion knowledge unless the motive was highly salient. Observers, who had
spare capacity, were more likely than the targets themselves to see the tactic for
what it was. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pc-pkm) summarises the mechanism.

```{r fig-pc-pkm, fig.cap = "Mechanism of the persuasion knowledge model. An agent's tactic leads to persuasion-motive inference only when persuasion knowledge is accessible and the target has capacity to use it. Recognition changes the tactic's meaning and shapes coping."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  T  [label = "Agent tactic\\n(flattery, endorsement,\\nscarcity claim)", %s]
  K  [label = "Persuasion knowledge\\n(folk theories of tactics)", %s]
  I  [label = "Inference of ulterior\\n(persuasion) motive", %s]
  C  [label = "Change of meaning:\\ntactic seen as manipulation\\nor as fair practice", %s]
  O  [label = "Coping response:\\ndiscounting, resistance,\\nreduced trust or acceptance", %s]
  A  [label = "Accessibility of\\nulterior motive", %s]
  Y  [label = "Cognitive capacity\\nof the target", %s]
  T -> I
  K -> I
  I -> C -> O
  A -> I [style = dashed]
  Y -> I [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome,
   node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

The PKM and the [ELM](#elaboration-likelihood-model) are complementary. Persuasion knowledge can be thought of as
one of the things people think *about* when they elaborate. A highly involved
target may scrutinise not only the arguments but also the agent's motives.
Recognising a manipulative intent can then produce counter-arguments and resistance.
Conversely, the PKM explains why peripheral cues sometimes fail: a celebrity
endorsement that is recognised as purchased may stop working as a cue of quality and
start working as a cue of persuasive intent.

### Evidence and extensions

The model has been used to study advertising literacy among children and
adolescents, covert marketing, product placement, native advertising, sales
interactions, and corporate social responsibility claims. A recurring finding is
that recognising persuasive intent is not uniformly harmful to the persuader.
When a tactic is judged appropriate, an honest disclosure, a transparent
comparison, recognition can increase perceived fairness and trust. When a tactic is
judged inappropriate, a hidden payment, a deceptive claim, recognition produces
discounting and a lasting penalty to agent knowledge ("this brand tries to trick
people"). The model therefore predicts asymmetric long-run consequences: the
short-run gains from covert tactics must be weighed against the costs incurred when
they are discovered.

::: {.business-case}
**Influencer marketing and sponsorship disclosure.** Influencer content is
persuasive in part because it looks like ordinary peer communication rather than
advertising. The PKM predicts that disclosing the commercial relationship, "#ad",
"paid partnership", "sponsored", activates persuasion knowledge, increasing the
likelihood that followers recognise the post as advertising. Regulators have
taken the same view: the US Federal Trade Commission's guidance on endorsements
requires that material connections between endorsers and brands be disclosed
clearly and conspicuously, and major platforms provide built-in paid-partnership
labels. For brands, the managerial question is not whether to disclose (that is a
legal obligation in many jurisdictions) but how to design partnerships that survive
disclosure. The model's answer is **fit and appropriateness**: when the influencer
plausibly uses and values the product, the persuasion motive is seen as compatible
with the influencer's genuine opinion. When the fit is poor, disclosure highlights
the payment and invites discounting. Several practical rules follow: choose
creators whose prior content demonstrates authentic topic knowledge, allow them to
express qualified opinions, and avoid scripts that read as advertising copy.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Sponsorship disclosure increases recognition of advertising, and this
  recognition mediates a decrease in source trustworthiness.
- *H2.* The negative effect of disclosure on brand attitude is attenuated when
  influencer-product fit is high.
- *H3.* Cognitive load reduces the effect of an inappropriate sales tactic on
  perceived manipulative intent [@campbell2000].

**Measures.** Advertising recognition, inferences of manipulative intent,
perceived appropriateness of tactics, source trustworthiness, resistance
(counter-arguing, sharing intentions).

**Designs.** Between-subject experiments varying disclosure presence, wording, and
position. Field experiments with platform disclosure labels. Eye tracking to measure
whether disclosures are noticed.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Assuming persuasion knowledge is always activated.** Many studies equate the
*presence* of a disclosure with *activation* of persuasion knowledge. Disclosures
that are small, late, or buried in hashtags may not be noticed. Measure recognition
directly, and remember that knowledge must be both available and accessible, and
the target must have capacity to use it.
:::

## Word of Mouth and Social Transmission {#social-transmission}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People share information, opinions, and content because sharing
serves their own needs: managing impressions, regulating emotions, acquiring
information, bonding with others, and persuading. These motives, together with
features of the content and the audience, determine *what* is shared and how far it
spreads.

**Origins.** Sociology of personal influence [@katz1955], marketing research on
word of mouth [@godes2004; @chevalier2006], synthesised in @berger2014 and
@Berger_2013.

**Level of analysis.** Individual sharer, dyad, and social network.

**Key constructs.** Word of mouth (WOM), sharer motives, content characteristics
(emotional arousal, practical value, social currency), audience size, triggers,
opinion leaders, cascades.

**Boundary conditions.** Predictions about content features assume people choose
what to share. Network position, platform algorithms, and paid amplification can
dominate content effects in some settings.

**Related theories.** [Emotion and virality](#emotion-and-virality) (Section \@ref(emotion-and-virality)),
[Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)), [Weak ties](#weak-ties) (Section \@ref(weak-ties)),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling) (Section \@ref(identity-signaling)), [Microblogging](#microblogging).
:::

### From mass media to personal influence: the two-step flow

The study of social transmission began with a surprise. When Lazarsfeld and his
colleagues studied how voters in Erie County, Ohio, made up their minds during the
1940 US presidential campaign, they expected to find strong direct effects of radio
and print media. Instead, they found that many voters reported being influenced by
other people, and that ideas often seemed to flow from the media to **opinion
leaders** and from them to less active sections of the population
[@lazarsfeld1944]. @katz1955 developed this **two-step flow** hypothesis in a study
of women in Decatur, Illinois, examining influence in marketing, fashion, public
affairs, and film-going. Opinion leaders were found at every social level, differed
by domain, and were distinguished by greater media exposure and by their social
position, not merely by status (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pc-twostep)).

```{r fig-pc-twostep, fig.cap = "The two-step flow of communication (Katz & Lazarsfeld, 1955) and its modern revision. Media content reaches opinion leaders, who interpret and relay it through interpersonal ties. Network research suggests that large cascades depend on many easily influenced individuals rather than a few influentials (Watts & Dodds, 2007)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  MM [label = "Mass media\\nand brand content", %s]
  OL [label = "Opinion leaders\\n(high exposure, domain\\ninterest, central ties)", %s]
  IP [label = "Interpersonal\\ninterpretation and\\nrecommendation", %s]
  F  [label = "Followers:\\nattitudes and adoption", %s]
  S  [label = "Susceptibility of\\nthe wider network", %s]
  MM -> OL [label = " step 1"]
  OL -> IP [label = " step 2"]
  IP -> F
  MM -> F [style = dashed, label = " weaker\\n direct path"]
  S -> F [style = dotted]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

The two-step flow shaped decades of marketing practice, from seeding products with
"influentials" to opinion-leader scales in consumer research. Later network research
has qualified it. In simulations of influence networks, @watts2007 found that large
cascades were usually driven not by a small number of highly influential people but
by a critical mass of easily influenced individuals. Influentials can trigger
cascades, but only when the network is ready. The practical implication is that
seeding strategy depends on network structure as much as on the identity of the
seed.

### Why people share

@berger2014 organises the literature around the **functions** that word of mouth
serves for the sharer. The framework explains why sharing is not a neutral relay of
information: what people choose to say reflects what the act of saying it does for
them (Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-wom-functions)).

```{r tab-pc-wom-functions}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Function, ~`What sharing does for the sharer`, ~`Predicted content features`, ~`Business implication`,
  "Impression management", "Signals identity, expertise, and status, supports self-enhancement", "Remarkable, novel, or insider content, positive self-relevant stories", "Give customers something that makes them look good to share",
  "Emotion regulation", "Generates social support, venting, sense-making, and reducing dissonance", "Emotionally intense experiences, positive and negative", "Expect negative WOM after service failures, offer channels to vent",
  "Information acquisition", "Seeks advice and resolves uncertainty", "Questions, requests for recommendations", "Be present where customers ask for advice",
  "Social bonding", "Reinforces shared views and reduces loneliness", "Common-ground content, shared experiences", "Design for communal experiences and conversation",
  "Persuasion", "Convinces others or changes their behaviour", "Arguments, strong opinions, polarised content", "Equip advocates with credible arguments"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Five functions of word of mouth (organised following Berger, 2014).")
```

Two further findings shape what spreads. First, **audience size** matters.
@barasch2014 showed that people who **broadcast** to many recipients focus on
self-presentation and avoid sharing content that makes them look bad, whereas people
who **narrowcast** to one recipient focus more on the recipient and share more useful
content. Second, sharing is **intrinsically rewarding**: in neuroimaging and
behavioural studies, @tamir2012 found that disclosing information about the self
engaged brain regions associated with reward, and that participants were willing
to forgo small monetary payments to talk about themselves.

### What gets shared: content characteristics

@berger2012 analysed which *New York Times* articles made the newspaper's
most-emailed list over a three-month period. Controlling for placement and other
features, positive content was more likely to be shared than negative content, but
emotion was not simply a matter of valence. Content evoking high-arousal emotions,
awe, anger, and anxiety, was more likely to be shared, whereas content evoking a
low-arousal emotion, sadness, was less likely to be shared. A complementary
experiment found that physiological arousal, even arousal induced by an unrelated
activity such as jogging in place, increased participants' willingness to share
content [@berger2011]. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-pc-arousal) places these emotions in
the valence-arousal space.

```{r fig-pc-arousal, fig.cap = "Conceptual map of emotions by valence and arousal, with the direction of their association with sharing reported by Berger & Milkman (2012) and Berger (2011). Positions are illustrative, not measured values.", fig.height = 4.2}
emo <- tibble::tribble(
  ~emotion, ~valence, ~arousal, ~sharing,
  "Awe", 0.70, 0.75, "More sharing",
  "Amusement", 0.60, 0.62, "More sharing",
  "Contentment", 0.55, 0.20, "Less sharing",
  "Anger", -0.70, 0.80, "More sharing",
  "Anxiety", -0.55, 0.68, "More sharing",
  "Sadness", -0.62, 0.18, "Less sharing"
)
ggplot(emo, aes(valence, arousal, colour = sharing)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = 1, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 1, fill = pal[["blue"]], alpha = 0.06) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = emotion), nudge_y = 0.055, size = 3.4, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.98, y = 0.97, label = "High arousal", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.98, y = 0.03, label = "Low arousal", hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("More sharing" = pal[["blue"]], "Less sharing" = pal[["orange"]]),
                      breaks = c("More sharing", "Less sharing")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = c(-0.8, 0, 0.8), labels = c("Negative", "Neutral", "Positive")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Valence", y = "Arousal", colour = "Association with sharing",
       title = "Arousal, not only valence, predicts sharing",
       caption = "Conceptual placement after Berger & Milkman (2012) and Berger (2011). Amusement and contentment from Berger (2011).")
```

Content characteristics also determine *when* sharing happens. @berger2011b found
that products that were more publicly visible and more frequently cued by the
environment received more word of mouth, and that interesting products received more
immediate but not more ongoing word of mouth. Environmental **triggers**, cues
that bring a product to mind, sustain conversation long after novelty fades.

### The STEPPS framework

For practitioners, @Berger_2013 synthesised this research into six principles,
summarised in Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-stepps). The framework is a checklist rather
than a formal theory, but each element maps onto a mechanism with independent
empirical support.

```{r tab-pc-stepps}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Principle, ~`Underlying mechanism`, ~`Design question`, ~`Illustrative tactic`,
  "Social currency", "Impression management, self-enhancement", "Does sharing make the sharer look good, smart, or in the know?", "Insider access, remarkable facts, game mechanics",
  "Triggers", "Accessibility, environmental cueing", "What in the everyday environment will bring this to mind?", "Link the product to a frequent context or time of day",
  "Emotion", "High-arousal emotion increases transmission", "Does the content evoke awe, amusement, anger, or anxiety?", "Focus on feelings rather than features",
  "Public", "Observability, social proof", "Can others see people using it?", "Visible packaging, shareable badges, branded artefacts",
  "Practical value", "Other-oriented helping, usefulness", "Is it useful enough to pass on?", "Tips, deals that are framed as unusual, how-to guides",
  "Stories", "Narrative transportation carries information", "Is the message embedded in a story people want to tell?", "Make the brand integral to the narrative, not an add-on"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The STEPPS framework for designing shareable content (Berger, 2013).")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Designing shareable content.** A consumer-electronics firm wants its product
launch to generate organic conversation rather than relying entirely on paid
media. Social transmission research suggests several design choices. To create
**social currency**, the launch might offer early access to a limited group, giving
those customers something remarkable to report. To create **triggers**, the firm
might tie the product to a recurring context, a commute, a weekly routine, so
that it is cued repeatedly after launch. The firm would aim for **high-arousal
emotion** (awe at a capability, amusement in a demonstration) rather than
low-arousal contentment. It would make use **public** through visible design or a
shareable output, and package **practical value** in tips that users would pass on
to help friends. Finally, it would embed the brand in a **story**, the problem a
customer solved, rather than adding a logo to unrelated entertainment. The theory
also flags risks: content optimised for arousal can attract anger as easily as awe,
and broadcast audiences reward self-presentation, so content that makes sharers look
foolish will not travel.
:::

### Word of mouth and market outcomes

Does word of mouth actually move sales? Field evidence suggests that it does, but
in ways that depend on the structure of conversation. @godes2004 found that the
*dispersion* of online conversations about television shows across different
communities was associated with subsequent ratings, suggesting that conversations
that cross social boundaries carry more new information than conversations within
one community. @chevalier2006 exploited differences in reviews between two online
booksellers and found that improvements in a book's reviews on one site were
associated with relative increases in its sales on that site, and that very
negative reviews had a larger effect than very positive ones. Both studies
illustrate a methodological challenge that recurs throughout this literature:
because word of mouth and sales are both driven by product quality, credible
identification requires comparison across sites, communities, or time.

### Misinformation and the spread of falsehood

Social transmission theory also illuminates why false information spreads.
@vosoughi2018 analysed the diffusion of roughly 126,000 rumour cascades on Twitter
from 2006 to 2017, classifying each as true or false using the verdicts of six
independent fact-checking organisations. Falsehood diffused significantly farther,
faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information,
and the effects were more pronounced for false political news than for other
categories. False stories were about 70% more likely to be retweeted than true ones.
Two findings bear directly on mechanism. First, false news was more **novel** than
true news, and replies to false stories expressed more surprise and disgust,
consistent with the view that novelty and emotional arousal drive sharing. Second,
automated accounts ("bots") accelerated the spread of true and false news at similar
rates, implying that the difference was driven by human sharing decisions rather
than by bots.

These findings connect directly to the functions of word of mouth. Novel
information confers social currency on the sharer. Arousing content is more likely
to be passed on, and broadcasting to many followers emphasises self-presentation
over careful verification. Correcting misinformation is difficult because of the
**continued influence effect**: retracted information often continues to shape
reasoning, especially when no alternative explanation is offered
[@lewandowsky2012]. Interventions that shift attention to accuracy at the moment of
sharing, for example, asking people to rate the accuracy of an unrelated headline,
have been found to improve the quality of news that people subsequently share,
including in a field experiment on Twitter [@pennycook2021].

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Content that evokes high-arousal emotions will be shared more than content
  evoking low-arousal emotions of the same valence [@berger2012].
- *H2.* The effect of social-currency features on sharing will be stronger when
  sharers broadcast to large audiences than when they narrowcast [@barasch2014].
- *H3.* Brands linked to frequent environmental triggers will receive more ongoing
  (but not more immediate) word of mouth [@berger2011b].

**Designs.** Archival analysis of shares, retweets, and reviews with content coded
by text analysis. Field experiments with seeding strategies. Laboratory
experiments that manipulate arousal or audience size. Natural experiments
created by platform changes.

**Measures.** Share counts and cascade depth, dispersion of conversation across
communities, sentiment and emotion dictionaries, self-reported sharing motives.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating virality as a property of content alone.** Whether content spreads
depends on content features *and* on network structure, platform ranking, paid
seeding, and timing. Studies that correlate content features with share counts
without accounting for exposure (how many people saw the content) confound the
probability of sharing with the opportunity to share. Normalise by exposure where
possible, and treat cascade size as a highly skewed outcome.
:::

## Microblogging and Undirected Communication {#microblogging}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Microblogging, status updates, posts, and short messages
broadcast to one's network, is valuable precisely because it is **undirected**: it
lets people reach out and invite social interaction without imposing communication
on any particular person.

**Origins.** Consumer psychology, @Buechel_2017.

**Level of analysis.** Individual communicator.

**Key constructs.** Directed versus undirected communication, social apprehension,
fear of rejection, social connection.

**Boundary conditions.** Most relevant where people have a choice between directed
channels (messages, calls) and undirected ones (public posts), and where the
audience is a loose network rather than a close dyad.

**Related theories.** [Social transmission](#social-transmission),
[Uses and gratifications](#uses-and-gratifications),
[Social comparison theory](#social-comparison-theory) (Section \@ref(social-comparison-theory)).
:::

Directed communication, a phone call, a direct message, an email to a specific
person, carries an implicit demand: the recipient is expected to respond. For
people who worry about being rejected or about imposing on others, that demand
creates a barrier to reaching out. @Buechel_2017 argue that undirected
communication removes the barrier. A status update is addressed to no one in
particular. Whoever responds does so voluntarily, so the poster can seek
interaction without the risk of a specific person declining it. Their studies
suggest that **socially apprehensive** individuals, those who are anxious about
communicating with others and concerned about rejection, find undirected
communication particularly attractive.

The insight complements the broader transmission literature. @barasch2014 showed
that audience size changes *what* people share. @Buechel_2017 show that directness
changes *whether* some people communicate at all. Research on why people post on
microblogging platforms also distinguishes intrinsic motives (enjoyment of posting)
from image-related motives (the status of having an audience). @toubia2013 found
evidence that image-related utility plays a substantial role for many
non-commercial users.

::: {.business-case}
**Community design and customer voice.** Brands that host customer communities
often find that a small share of members post while most only read. Undirected
communication research suggests one reason and one remedy. Directed requests ("Ask
an expert", "Message our team") may deter socially apprehensive customers, whereas
low-stakes undirected formats, open threads, reactions, "share your setup" posts,
let them participate without making a specific demand on anyone. The same logic
applies inside organisations: enterprise social platforms can surface questions from
employees who would hesitate to email a senior colleague directly. Designers should
pair such formats with norms that make responses likely, because an undirected post
that receives no response can itself feel like rejection.
:::

## Agenda Setting {#agenda-setting}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The news media may not tell people *what to think*, but they are
highly influential in telling people *what to think about*: the issues that
receive the most coverage come to be seen by the public as the most important.

**Origins.** Political communication, @mccombs1972, building on @cohen1963 and on
the voter studies of @lazarsfeld1944, extended to priming by @iyengar1987.

**Level of analysis.** Society and public opinion (aggregate issue salience).
Individual (issue importance judgments).

**Key constructs.** Media agenda, public agenda, issue salience, obtrusive versus
unobtrusive issues, need for orientation, attribute (second-level) agenda setting,
priming.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for **unobtrusive** issues that people cannot
observe directly (foreign policy, macroeconomic trends) and among people with a
high **need for orientation**. Weaker for issues experienced first-hand. Fragmented
and personalised media environments complicate the notion of a single media agenda.

**Related theories.** [Framing](#framing-theory),
[Spiral of silence](#spiral-of-silence) (Section \@ref(spiral-of-silence)), [Pack journalism](#pack-journalism) (Section \@ref(pack-journalism)),
[Availability heuristic](#heuristics-biases) (Section \@ref(heuristics-biases)).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

@cohen1963 observed that the press may often fail to tell people what to think but
is remarkably successful in telling them what to think about. @mccombs1972 turned
this observation into a testable hypothesis. During the 1968 US presidential
campaign, they surveyed undecided voters in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, about
which issues they considered most important, and content-analysed the news media
those voters used. The rank order of issues on the media agenda corresponded closely
to the rank order on the voters' agenda. Because undecided voters lacked strong
partisan filters, they were a sensible population in which to look for media
influence.

The correlational design left open the direction of causality: do media follow
the public or lead it?and later work used time-series designs and experiments to
address the question. @iyengar1987 manipulated the content of television news
broadcasts that participants watched over several days and found that issues
emphasised in the broadcasts became more important to viewers. They also documented
**priming**: issues that were made salient became more heavily weighted in viewers'
evaluations of the president. Agenda setting therefore has two consequences:
it shapes which issues people think are important, and it shapes which criteria
people use to evaluate leaders, firms, and products.

Later research distinguished **first-level** agenda setting (salience of objects
such as issues or candidates) from **attribute** or **second-level** agenda setting
(salience of particular attributes of those objects). Attribute agenda setting
overlaps with framing, and @scheufele2007 argue that agenda setting and priming
rest on accessibility, making some considerations easier to retrieve, whereas
framing rests on applicability: the fit between a frame and how an issue is
interpreted. Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-media-effects) summarises the distinction.

```{r tab-pc-media-effects}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Media effect`, ~`What media change`, ~`Psychological mechanism`, ~`Classic study`, ~`Business analogue`,
  "Agenda setting", "Perceived importance of issues", "Accessibility (salience)", "McCombs & Shaw (1972)", "Which attributes buyers consider at all",
  "Priming", "Criteria used to evaluate actors", "Accessibility of evaluative standards", "Iyengar & Kinder (1987)", "Which attribute dominates brand evaluation",
  "Framing", "Interpretation of an issue", "Applicability of an interpretive schema", "Entman (1993), Tversky & Kahneman (1981)", "How a price, risk, or crisis is understood"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Agenda setting, priming, and framing distinguished (following Scheufele & Tewksbury, 2007).")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Issue salience and corporate communication.** Agenda setting implies that firms
compete not only on positions but on *which issues are discussed at all*. A
manufacturer whose products excel on safety benefits when safety dominates media
coverage of its category, while a rival that leads on price benefits when
affordability dominates. Corporate communication functions therefore track media
agendas, invest in research and data releases that journalists cover, and time
announcements around the news cycle. The priming corollary is equally important:
during a public debate about data privacy, consumers may weight privacy more heavily
when evaluating a technology brand, even if their underlying preferences have not
changed. Firms whose reputations rest on an attribute that becomes salient should
expect amplified effects: positive or negative.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating coverage with persuasion.** Agenda setting is about salience, not about
direction of opinion. Heavy coverage of an issue can raise its importance while
leaving attitudes toward it unchanged, or while polarising them. Research that
treats volume of coverage as a measure of favourable influence conflates agenda
setting with persuasion.
:::

## Framing Theory {#framing-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The way information is presented, which aspects are emphasised,
and whether logically equivalent outcomes are described as gains or losses,
systematically changes judgments and choices.

**Origins.** Two traditions: behavioural decision research on **equivalence
framing** [@tversky1981; @levin1998], and communication and sociology research on
**emphasis framing** [@entman1993].

**Level of analysis.** Individual (choice and judgment) and societal (public
discourse).

**Key constructs.** Gain versus loss frames, risky-choice, attribute, and goal
framing, frame selection and salience, problem definition, causal interpretation,
moral evaluation, treatment recommendation.

**Boundary conditions.** Equivalence-framing effects are strongest when people do
not spontaneously translate between frames and when the decision is unfamiliar.
Emphasis-framing effects are weaker when audiences hold strong prior attitudes or
encounter competing frames.

**Related theories.** [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)),
[Agenda setting](#agenda-setting), [Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Anchoring](#anchoring-effect) (Section \@ref(anchoring-effect)).
:::

### Equivalence framing

@tversky1981 presented participants with the "Asian disease problem". An outbreak
is expected to kill 600 people, and participants choose between two programmes. In
one version, outcomes are described in terms of lives saved: Programme A will save
200 people for certain, whereas Programme B offers a one-third probability of saving
all 600 and a two-thirds probability of saving no one. In a second version, the same
outcomes are described in terms of deaths: under Programme C, 400 people will die
for certain. Under Programme D, there is a one-third probability that nobody will
die and a two-thirds probability that all 600 will die. The programmes are
numerically identical across versions, yet preferences reverse (Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-pc-asian-disease)). In the gain frame most participants chose the
certain option. In the loss frame most chose the gamble. The pattern follows from
[prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)): a value function that is concave for gains and
convex for losses produces risk aversion in the domain of gains and risk seeking in
the domain of losses.

```{r fig-pc-asian-disease, fig.cap = "The framing of decisions. Percentages choosing the certain versus the risky programme in the Asian disease problem, as reported by Tversky & Kahneman (1981). The gain-frame problem was answered by 152 respondents and the loss-frame problem by 155.", fig.height = 3.6}
asian <- tibble::tribble(
  ~frame, ~option, ~pct,
  "Gain frame (lives saved)", "Certain option", 72,
  "Gain frame (lives saved)", "Risky option", 28,
  "Loss frame (lives lost)", "Certain option", 22,
  "Loss frame (lives lost)", "Risky option", 78
) |>
  mutate(frame = factor(frame, levels = c("Gain frame (lives saved)", "Loss frame (lives lost)")))
ggplot(asian, aes(frame, pct, fill = option)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Certain option" = pal[["blue"]], "Risky option" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 88), expand = c(0, 0), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of respondents", fill = NULL,
       title = "Equivalent outcomes, opposite choices",
       caption = "Source: percentages reported in Tversky & Kahneman (1981).")
```

@levin1998 distinguish three types of equivalence framing that differ in what is
framed and in what they affect (Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-frames)). The distinction
matters because the types have different mechanisms and different typical effect
directions. **Attribute framing** is the most common in marketing: in a classic
study, ground beef described as "75% lean" was rated more favourably than beef
described as "25% fat", and the difference was attenuated, though not eliminated,
after participants tasted the meat [@levin1988].

```{r tab-pc-frames}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Frame type`, ~`What is framed`, ~`What is affected`, ~`Typical effect`, ~Example,
  "Risky-choice framing", "Outcomes of options with different risk levels", "Risk preference", "Risk aversion for gains, risk seeking for losses", "Asian disease problem",
  "Attribute framing", "A single attribute of an object", "Evaluation of the object", "Positive labels yield more favourable evaluations", "\"75% lean\" vs. \"25% fat\"",
  "Goal framing", "Consequences of performing or not performing an act", "Persuasiveness of an appeal", "Loss frames often more persuasive", "\"You lose X by not insulating\" vs. \"You gain X by insulating\""
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Three types of equivalence framing (Levin, Schneider, & Gaeth, 1998).")
```

### Emphasis framing

In communication research, framing refers less to logically equivalent descriptions
and more to *selection and emphasis*. @entman1993 defined framing as selecting some
aspects of a perceived reality and making them more salient in a communicating text
so as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral
evaluation, and/or treatment recommendation. A news report about rising fuel prices
can frame the issue as a problem of corporate profits, of geopolitical supply, of
environmental policy, or of household budgets: each frame highlighting different
causes and remedies. Entman's four functions provide a coding scheme widely used in
content analysis: does the text define a problem, diagnose causes, make a moral
judgment, and suggest a remedy?

The two traditions are complementary rather than competing. Equivalence framing
shows that even *logically identical* information can change choices. Emphasis
framing shows that the selection of *which* true considerations to foreground shapes
interpretation. Both are pervasive in business communication: in pricing ("less than
a dollar a day"), in risk communication ("99% success rate" versus "1% failure
rate"), and in organisational change ("restructuring for growth" versus "cost
cutting").

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Crisis communication and framing.** When a crisis threatens a firm's reputation,
stakeholders ask who is responsible. **Situational crisis communication theory**
[@coombs2007] builds on [attribution theory](#attribution-theory) (Section \@ref(attribution-theory)) to argue that the appropriate response
depends on how much responsibility stakeholders attribute to the organisation. Crises
in the *victim* cluster (natural disasters, product tampering by outsiders) attract
little attribution of responsibility. *Accidental* crises (technical errors) attract
moderate attribution. *Preventable* crises (management misconduct, known risks that
were ignored) attract strong attribution. Response strategies range from **deny**
(attack the accuser, deny the crisis) through **diminish** (excuse, justification) to
**rebuild** (compensation, apology). Framing is central: the firm's first
communications shape which cluster stakeholders assign the crisis to. Johnson &
Johnson's response to the 1982 Tylenol poisonings, a nationwide recall and the
introduction of tamper-resistant packaging, despite the poisonings having been
caused by an outside criminal, is widely taught as a case in which the firm framed
itself as acting to protect customers rather than as a defendant. The theory also
warns against mismatches: a firm that uses a "victim" frame for a crisis the public
perceives as preventable invites further reputational damage.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Describing a product attribute in positive terms ("90% success") will
  increase evaluations relative to the equivalent negative description ("10% failure"),
  and the effect will be smaller for experts.
- *H2.* In crisis communication, rebuild strategies will protect reputation more than
  deny strategies when stakeholders attribute high responsibility to the firm
  [@coombs2007].
- *H3.* News articles that frame a corporate event using a "moral" frame will generate
  more negative social-media sentiment than articles using an "economic" frame.

**Designs.** Randomised framing experiments. Content analysis of news and
social-media frames (manual coding or supervised text classification). Event
studies of market reactions to differently framed announcements.

**Measures.** Choice shares, risk preferences, evaluations, frame-coding schemes
based on Entman's four functions, attributions of responsibility.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling every message difference a "frame".** If two messages differ in the
information they contain, not just in its presentation or emphasis, differences in
outcome may reflect information rather than framing. Equivalence-framing designs
require logically equivalent descriptions. Emphasis-framing designs should hold
facts constant and vary only which considerations are foregrounded.
:::

## Uses and Gratifications {#uses-and-gratifications}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Audiences are active and goal-directed: people select media and
content to satisfy needs, and the effects of media depend on the gratifications
people seek and obtain.

**Origins.** Mass-communication research, @katz1973, @blumler1974, updated for
digital media by @ruggiero2000.

**Level of analysis.** Individual audience member.

**Key constructs.** Social and psychological needs, expectations of media,
gratifications sought, gratifications obtained, media choice, functional
alternatives (non-media sources of gratification).

**Boundary conditions.** Assumes people are aware of, and can report, their motives.
Habitual and algorithmically curated media use may weaken the assumption of
deliberate selection.

**Related theories.** [Self-determination theory](#self-determination-theory) (Section \@ref(self-determination-theory)),
[Microblogging](#microblogging), [Social transmission](#social-transmission),
[Technology acceptance model](#technology-acceptance-model) (Section \@ref(technology-acceptance-model)).
:::

### Core logic

Most media-effects theories ask what media do to people. **Uses and
gratifications** reverses the question and asks what people do with media.
@katz1973 summarised the approach in a set of assumptions: the audience is active
and its media use is goal-directed. The initiative in linking need gratification to
media choice lies with the audience member. Media compete with other sources of
need satisfaction. People are sufficiently self-aware to report their interests and
motives, and value judgments about the cultural significance of media should be
suspended while audience orientations are explored. The approach locates the
origin of media effects in the social and psychological needs that generate
expectations of media and lead to differential patterns of exposure.

Table \@ref(tab:tab-pc-ug) summarises a typology of gratifications commonly used in
the literature, with contemporary business examples. The categories overlap, and
the same medium can serve several of them at once.

```{r tab-pc-ug}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Gratification, ~`Underlying need`, ~`Traditional media example`, ~`Digital and business example`,
  "Information / surveillance", "Understanding the environment, reducing uncertainty", "News bulletins", "Product reviews, industry newsletters",
  "Personal identity", "Reinforcing values, self-understanding", "Lifestyle magazines", "Following creators who express one's identity",
  "Integration and social interaction", "Belonging, conversation material", "Watching the same broadcast as friends", "Brand communities, group chats, live-streams",
  "Entertainment / diversion", "Escape, relaxation, emotional release", "Television drama", "Short-video platforms, mobile games",
  "Self-expression and status", "Being seen, building an audience", "Letters to the editor", "Posting reviews, microblogging"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "A typology of media gratifications with business examples.")
```

### Evidence, extensions, and critique

The approach has proved adaptable. Each new medium, radio, television, the
internet, mobile phones, social networks, has been studied by asking which needs
it serves and how it competes with older media. @ruggiero2000 argued that the
interactivity, demassification, and asynchroneity of digital media make the active
audience assumption more plausible than in the broadcast era, and that uses and
gratifications would become more rather than less relevant. Critics have long
noted that the approach can be descriptive and individualistic: lists of
gratifications proliferate, self-reports of motives may be post-hoc
rationalisations, and the theory says less about the content and institutional
structure of media than about audience motives. Habitual use and recommendation
algorithms also complicate the claim that media choice reflects deliberate goals.

::: {.debate}
**Active audience or captured attention?** Uses and gratifications assumes that
people choose media to satisfy needs. Critics of engagement-optimised platforms
argue that recommendation systems shape the needs they then satisfy, so that what
looks like goal-directed choice is partly the product of design. One way to reconcile
the views is to distinguish **gratifications sought** from **gratifications
obtained**: a platform may attract users by promising social connection
(gratification sought) while delivering mainly diversion (gratification obtained).
Persistent gaps between the two predict dissatisfaction and churn: a testable
implication with clear managerial relevance.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Content strategy by gratification.** A business-to-business software company
publishes a blog, a podcast, and a community forum. Uses and gratifications suggests
assessing each channel by the needs it serves rather than by reach alone. The blog
might serve *information* needs (how-to guides), the podcast *personal identity*
and *diversion* needs (listening to respected practitioners during a commute), and
the forum *social interaction* and *self-expression* needs (helping peers, building
a reputation). Metrics follow from the gratification: search traffic and task
completion for information content, completion rates and subscriptions for the
podcast, and contribution rates and reciprocal replies for the forum. Content that
fails to deliver the gratification its audience seeks, a promotional podcast
episode, an unanswered forum post, erodes use even if it is widely distributed.
:::

::: {.try-it}
List the three apps or media you used most yesterday. For each, write down the
gratification you sought when you opened it and the gratification you actually
obtained. Where they diverge, what design feature of the medium explains the gap,
and what would a firm need to change to close it?
:::

## Chapter Summary {#persuasion-communication-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- Persuasion depends on **how much people think**. Under high elaboration,
  argument quality dominates. Under low elaboration, peripheral cues and heuristics
  dominate, and the resulting attitudes are weaker [@petty1986; @chaiken1980].
- Audiences recognise and cope with persuasion. The **persuasion knowledge model**
  explains why disclosed or recognised tactics can change meaning and lose force,
  and why appropriate tactics can survive disclosure [@friestad1994; @campbell2000].
- People share because sharing serves **their own functions**: impression
  management, emotion regulation, information, bonding, and persuasion
  [@berger2014]. High-arousal content travels further [@berger2012].
- Influence flows through **people as well as media** [@katz1955], but large
  cascades depend on network susceptibility more than on a few influentials
  [@watts2007].
- **Undirected communication** such as microblogging lets people reach out
  without imposing on anyone in particular [@Buechel_2017].
- Falsehood spreads farther and faster than truth, driven by human sharing of novel,
  arousing content [@vosoughi2018].
- Media shape **what people think about** (agenda setting) and which criteria they
  use (priming) [@mccombs1972; @iyengar1987]. **Framing** shapes how issues and
  choices are interpreted [@tversky1981; @entman1993].
- **Uses and gratifications** treats audiences as goal-directed and explains media
  choice by the needs it serves [@katz1973].
:::

## Discussion Questions {#persuasion-communication-questions}

1. The ELM predicts that argument-based attitudes are more durable than cue-based
   attitudes. Design a field experiment for a consumer brand that would test this
   prediction using purchase data rather than self-reported attitudes.
2. A regulator proposes that all influencer posts carry a prominent "Advertisement"
   label. Using the persuasion knowledge model, predict the effects on followers,
   influencers, and brands, and identify the conditions under which disclosure would
   *not* reduce persuasion.
3. @vosoughi2018 found that falsehood spreads farther than truth. Which functions of
   word of mouth help explain this pattern, and what platform design changes would
   follow from each?
4. Agenda setting was first documented in an era of a few dominant news outlets. How
   would you test the theory in a fragmented, algorithmically curated media
   environment? What is "the media agenda" in that setting?
5. Distinguish equivalence framing from emphasis framing. Give one business example
   of each, and explain how you would design an experiment that isolates the framing
   effect from an information effect.
6. Choose a product category. Using uses and gratifications, identify the dominant
   gratification sought by its customers and propose a content strategy that serves
   it. How would you measure whether the gratification is obtained?

## Further Reading {#persuasion-communication-reading}

- @petty1986: the definitive statement of the elaboration likelihood model, its
  postulates, and the early evidence.
- @petty1983: the canonical advertising experiment showing the involvement ×
  argument quality × peripheral cue pattern.
- @friestad1994: the original persuasion knowledge model. Essential for research on
  disclosure, covert marketing, and sales tactics.
- @berger2014: a comprehensive review of word of mouth organised around the
  functions sharing serves.
- @berger2012: an influential empirical study of which content goes viral and why
  arousal matters.
- @vosoughi2018: a large-scale analysis of how true and false news spread online.
- @scheufele2007: a clear conceptual comparison of agenda setting, priming, and
  framing.
- @katz1973: the foundational statement of the uses and gratifications approach.
